headline: ML models for omics and drug response prediction gain calibration and interpretability
label: Machine Learning For Biomolecular Prediction
summary: Recent work tests whether simple, calibrated, or interpretable models match complex architectures for omics and drug-response prediction.
synthesis: The common thread is evaluation discipline over architectural novelty. Several items show that simple models remain competitive: a KNN over biological knowledge graphs predicts unseen gene knockout transcriptomic responses, and Rhaister predicts drug and perturbation responses from screen-level summary statistics. Others add reliability layers, including split conformal prediction for calibrated patient-level AML drug response intervals, an XGBoost quality score for chromatin accessibility tracks, and inter-sample consistency for evaluating single-cell cell type annotations without ground truth. Benchmarking and interpretability recur as well, with six LLMs assessed for cell-free RNA biomarker discovery and Rashomon-set rules applied to low-sample multi-omics. What is new is the focus on whether predictions can be trusted, compared against baselines, and traced to specific molecules. The thread does not extend to every item; GLEAM addresses code-free ML tooling and markeR addresses gene-set evaluation for senescence.
